Maria — thanks for sending the redlines and the heads-up on timing. Quick answers up front, followed by proposed language:

- Notification window: Redwood's standard is 30 days for non-critical additions, 10 days for critical security infrastructure updates (we typically try to avoid the latter but need the flexibility). We can commit to a 30-day notification window for new subprocessors that process customer data, with a carve-out for emergency security patches (we'll notify as soon as practicable and explain the reason).

- Objection process: our standard procedure is a 15-business-day review window from date of notice for the customer to raise objections. If an objection is raised, Redwood will engage in good-faith remediation discussions for up to 30 business days; if remediation is not possible and the objection relates to material breach/compliance risk, the customer may request removal or transition assistance.

- E-sign: we use DocuSign for standard DPA execution. I attached our current subprocessor list and the standard DPA terms for your review (Subprocessors_2026-07-11.csv; Redwood_DPA_Std_Terms_v3.docx). I can generate a DocuSign envelope once we align on the objection window and any carve-outs.

Proposed redline snippet you can paste into your DPA: 
"Customer will be notified at least 30 days in advance of the addition of any Subprocessor that will process Customer Data. In emergency circumstances (e.g., urgent security patches), Redwood may provide shorter notice but will notify Customer as soon as reasonably practicable and provide an explanation. Upon receipt of notice, Customer shall have 15 business days to raise an objection to the proposed Subprocessor. If Customer raises an objection, both parties will engage in good faith discussions for up to 30 business days to address the objection, which may include additional safeguards, contract terms with the Subprocessor, or alternative implementation plans. If remediation is not feasible and the objection concerns a material legal/compliance risk, Customer may require Redwood to cease the use of the Subprocessor with appropriate transition assistance."

Thoughts? If that's acceptable I will generate the DocuSign envelope and propose a sign-by date of Tue, Jul 20 to keep your procurement cycle on track.

Best,

Soojin — quick thoughts from Sales: don't agree to a blanket unilateral cancellation right that could be invoked for any perceived risk — that creates operational churn. Propose we accept a removal right only where there's a documented regulatory/legal finding or a material data breach tied to the Subprocessor. For other objections, offer a mitigation plan and time-bound remedies (e.g., extra logging, contractual assurances with the Subprocessor). If Acme insists on termination rights in more cases, we should require a transition/exit plan and a 60-day notice for service-impacting removals.

We can accept the 5-business-day incident summary for emergency additions but make the summary an operational report (facts-only) and limit legal admission language.

If legal and I can sync on precise wording, I'm happy to push this through — keeping Jul 20 sign date is preferred.
